lesson.title: Boxing Up the Five-Number Summary: How to Read and Build a Boxplot
lesson.summary: A boxplot turns the five-number summary into a picture, using a box for the middle 50 percent of the data and whiskers to show the rest, while flagging unusually extreme values as separate outlier points.
lesson.body:
A boxplot, sometimes called a box-and-whisker plot, is a graph built directly from the five-number summary. A rectangular box stretches from Q1 to Q3, capturing the middle 50 percent of the data, with a line drawn inside the box at the median. From each end of the box, a whisker extends outward toward the minimum and maximum values, unless those extreme values are flagged as outliers, in which case the whisker stops at the last value that is not an outlier and the outlier is marked as a separate dot or asterisk.

Deciding what counts as an outlier is not a guess. Statisticians use the 1.5 times IQR rule: first compute the IQR, then find a lower fence at Q1 minus 1.5 times IQR and an upper fence at Q3 plus 1.5 times IQR. Any data value falling outside those two fences is flagged as an outlier and plotted individually, while the whiskers stretch only to the most extreme values that remain inside the fences.

Consider the home run totals of eleven players on a team's roster: 5, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 35. With n equal to 11, an odd number, the median is the 6th value, which is 12. The lower half, excluding the median, is 5, 8, 9, 10, 11, and its median, the 3rd value, is 9. That is Q1. The upper half is 13, 14, 15, 16, 35, and its median, the 3rd value, is 15. That is Q3. The IQR is 15 minus 9, or 6, so 1.5 times IQR is 9. That gives a lower fence of Q1 minus 9, which is 9 minus 9, or 0, and an upper fence of Q3 plus 9, which is 15 plus 9, or 24.

Every value in the data set is at least 0, so nothing is flagged as a low outlier, and the lower whisker reaches all the way to the actual minimum, 5. On the high end, though, 35 is well above the upper fence of 24, so it is flagged as an outlier and drawn as a separate point. The upper whisker stops instead at 16, the largest value that is not an outlier. The finished boxplot shows a box from 9 to 15 with a line at 12, a whisker down to 5, a whisker up to 16, and a lone dot at 35 representing a player whose home run total was unusually high compared to the rest of the roster.

It is worth noticing what the outlier actually reveals here. Without the 1.5 times IQR rule, a whisker stretching all the way to 35 would have suggested the whole roster's home run totals were spread very widely, from 5 up to 35. By separating that single unusual value out as a flagged outlier, the boxplot instead makes clear that ten of the eleven players are clustered fairly closely between 5 and 16, and that 35 is an exceptional case worth investigating on its own, perhaps a star player having a breakout season, rather than treating it as just another ordinary data point.

Boxplots earn their place in a statistics toolkit because they show center, spread, and outliers all in one compact picture, and because several boxplots can be stacked side by side on the same scale to compare groups directly. What a boxplot cannot show clearly is the fine detail of shape, such as whether the data has one peak or several, which is where a histogram becomes the better tool. Used together, the two graphs complement each other when the next step is comparing entire distributions rather than describing just one.
